web_title: 3. Cash Conversion, Working Capital & the Raw-Material Chain
question: When the profit is reported, how much of it arrives as cash, and what has to stay true in the supply chain for that to continue?

epigraph.quote: We do not have long term supply contracts with our raw material suppliers, and therefore, we are subject to the risk of increases in the costs of raw materials.
epigraph.author: Stallion Red Herring Prospectus, risk factors, 11 January 2025 [6]

web_blocks.html: Profit is an opinion until the cash arrives. For a refrigerant business the cash story runs through three places: the raw material bought from abroad, the inventory held to meet orders, and the credit given to customers. This chapter follows each one through the FY26 audited figures and the RHP’s disclosures, and it tests two bear points against the filings.

web_blocks.title: Where the raw material comes from

web_blocks.html: The raw-material side is the largest and least secure part of the chain. The RHP says import costs were 85.00% of revenue from operations in the six months to September 2024, up from 70.23% in FY23 [6]. China supplied 92.97% of those imports in the same period [6]. The RHP is direct about what follows: “We do not have long term supply contracts with our raw material suppliers, and therefore, we are subject to the risk of increases in the costs of raw materials.” [6]

On the August 2026 call, an analyst asked about sourcing, and management’s answer shows why the contract gap matters. Management said: “Now to have anything to have value has to be iron-clad. And iron-clad will mean time-bound supply after which the penalties start enhancing. So it’s not in the best interest of the company.” [9] It also expected a glut of AHF supply by 2028, which it called a buyer’s market [9]. Both are management’s views. The sources contain no supply contract behind either one.

web_blocks.title: The FY26 cost waterfall, per ₹100 of revenue

web_blocks.html: The waterfall takes FY26 audited revenue from operations of ₹430.68 crore and scales every line to ₹100 of revenue. It reconciles to audited profit after tax of ₹43.84 crore, so each line is an audited figure and no line is estimated.

web_blocks.caption: Audited FY26 cost waterfall, scaled to ₹100 of revenue from operations

lines.label: Change in inventories
lines.note: Audited change in inventories of −₹2,395.94 lakh, booked as a credit to cost because inventory rose [1]

web_blocks.takeaway: Materials take ₹85.70 of every ₹100 of revenue. The inventory credit adds back ₹5.56, and tax takes ₹3.52. What is left is ₹10.18 of profit after tax. The statements give no product-level split, so this margin is for the company as a whole.

web_blocks.html: The inventory credit is the line to watch. The ₹23.96 crore credit to cost came from holding more finished inventory at the end of the year than at the start [1]. The cost sits on the balance sheet until that inventory is sold, so the margin benefits in the year the inventory is built and the cost lands later. On the August call, an analyst asked how much of the quarter’s EBITDA came from inventory gains. Management replied: “It’s a mix, 50:50.” [9] That is an answer about one quarter, not the full year, and no filing gives the split.

Put a number on the raw-material exposure. The FY26 waterfall has materials at about ₹85.70 of every ₹100 of revenue, and profit after tax at about ₹10.18 [1]. So a rise of 1% in material cost alone, before any pass-through to customers, takes about ₹0.86 of profit out of every ₹100 of revenue. That is roughly 8% of the year’s profit from a single percentage point. With no long-term contract, the company carries that sensitivity itself.

web_blocks.title: Working capital: customers paid faster, inventory stayed heavy

web_blocks.html: Trade receivables fell from ₹105.54 crore at March 2025 to ₹77.53 crore at March 2026 [1]. Inventory at March 2026 was ₹126.63 crore, and the audited change in inventories shows it rose by about ₹24 crore over the year [1]. The ratio series shows the effect in days. Debtor days fell from 102 to 66, while inventory days edged up from 128 to 134 [24]. Days payable fell from 27 to 19, so the company now pays its suppliers faster than it did a year earlier [24].

Put the days into money, roughly. FY26 revenue of ₹430.68 crore works out to about ₹1.18 crore of sales a day. The 36-day fall in debtor days is therefore worth roughly ₹42 crore of cash, released once. That is a real gain, but it does not repeat every year, so the next gain has to come from sales or margin [1][24].

web_blocks.caption: Working capital days, years to 31 March (Screener ratio series)
rows: Inventory held slightly longer again in FY26
Cycle shortened by 23 days in FY26
web_blocks.takeaway: The 23-day shortening came mostly from customers paying faster, a 36-day gain. Suppliers being paid sooner and inventory held longer took back about 14 days of that. The cycle is shorter, but the inventory line is not improving.

web_blocks.title: A BEAR POINT THE FILINGS DO NOT SUPPORT
paragraphs: A common bear point says receivables jumped in FY26. The audited balance sheet shows the opposite. Trade receivables fell from ₹105.54 crore to ₹77.53 crore [1]. What did rise sharply is cash and bank balances. Cash and cash equivalents were ₹212.47 crore and bank balances were ₹221.20 crore at March 2026, both after the rights issue [1][23].
Keep the two claims apart. A rise in receivables would mean customers were taking longer to pay. The filings show the reverse, so the bear point should be rewritten rather than repeated.

web_blocks.title: Cash conversion: profit that arrived as cash

web_blocks.html: Operating cash flow was ₹39.36 crore in FY26, against profit after tax of ₹43.84 crore. That is a conversion of about 0.90 times, a good year for this business. The two years before it were not good. Operating cash flow was negative ₹73 crore in FY24 and negative ₹13.43 crore in FY25, although profit after tax was positive in both years [14][1][4].

Cash is the test of whether a profit is real, and one good year does not settle it. Weak conversion in the earlier years came while the business was building receivables and inventory, which is how a profit can be recorded and not collected. FY26 is the first year in this record where operating cash came close to profit. Earlier, FY22 conversion was about 0.38 times on the same Screener series [24].

web_blocks.title: Capex and fixed deposits: where the cash went

web_blocks.html: The cash-flow summary shows investing outflows of about ₹253 crore in FY26 [14]. Most of it was not spent on plants. Net placements into fixed deposits came to ₹205.13 crore [23]. Spending on property, plant and equipment, capital work in progress and intangibles was ₹49.31 crore [23]. A reading that treats the whole ₹253 crore as plant spending would overstate capex by about five times, so keep the two lines apart when you read the capex story in later chapters.

The bigger capex question is what was committed, not what was spent. The RHP set aside ₹29.16 crore for the Khalapur specialty-gas facility and ₹21.18 crore for the Mambattu refrigerant plant out of the offer [5]. The FY26 annual report puts the planned HFO plant at about ₹200 crore [2], and the August call put it at ₹350 to ₹400 crore [9]. Those commitments are several times the ₹49 crore of plant spending in FY26, so the next two years of capex are where the plan will be tested.

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR’S REFLECTION
paragraphs: Pause on the cash cycle. A business that cut its debtor days by 36 in one year has done something real. Ask whether it came from a change in policy, a change in customer mix, or timing around the rights issue. The filings do not say, and you should not assume the answer.

Hold the import number next to it. Most of the cost sits in one country’s supply, with no long-term contract to protect the company when that cost moves. Good working capital helps a company survive a bad quarter. It does not protect the margin.

book_paragraphs: Let me start with a simple question. When the company reports a profit, how much of it do you actually receive in cash? For a refrigerant business that question is not academic. The business buys its main raw material from abroad, holds inventory so it can meet orders, and gives customers time to pay. Each of those three steps ties up money, and each can turn a profit on paper into a shortage in the bank.

The raw material is the first thing to understand. The RHP says import costs were 85 percent of revenue in the six months to September 2024, up from about 70 percent in FY23. China supplied almost all of the imports in that period, at 92.97 percent. And the company says plainly that it has no long-term supply contracts with those suppliers. So when the cost of the raw material moves, the company moves with it. Management, when asked on the August call, described why it had not signed fixed contracts. It said a contract with no real penalty has no value, and it did not want to sign one that did not bind anyone. You can agree or disagree with that view, but you should notice that the protection is not in place today.

Now look at the FY26 waterfall. Take every rupee of revenue and see where it goes. Of each hundred rupees of revenue, about eighty-six went on materials. The inventory build gave back about five and a half, because the company held more finished product at year end. Employees, other costs, interest and depreciation took a few more. Tax took about three and a half. What was left was about ten rupees of profit after tax. That is a thin margin on a large base of purchased material, and it is why a small move in input cost matters so much.

The inventory credit deserves a careful look. When inventory rises, the cost of the goods you have not yet sold sits on the balance sheet, and that lifts the reported margin in the year it happens. It does not stay there forever. Management was asked on the August call how much of the quarter’s earnings came from inventory gains, and it said the split was about fifty-fifty. That is an answer about one quarter. It tells you the company itself sees a real share of its earnings coming from timing, and that the full-year split is not in any filing.

The working capital story has a good half and a stronger-looking half that is not what it seems. Customers paid faster. Debtor days fell from 102 to 66 in one year, and trade receivables dropped from about 106 crore to about 78 crore. That is the part to celebrate. Inventory days, however, did not improve. They went from 128 to 134. The company is holding its inventory as long as before, and it is paying suppliers more quickly, which takes back some of the gain. Put together, the cash cycle shortened from 203 days to 180. Shorter is better, but the cycle is shorter for reasons you should be able to name.

There is a bear point circulating that says receivables jumped in FY26. The audited balance sheet says the opposite. Receivables fell. What rose sharply was cash and bank balances, after the rights issue money came in. If you hear someone say the company is struggling to collect what it is owed, ask for the balance-sheet line. It will not support that claim, and it is better to say so plainly than to repeat it.

The test of all this is cash conversion. In FY26 operating cash flow was about 39 crore, against profit after tax of about 44 crore. That is a conversion of roughly nine tenths, and it is the best the record shows. Two years earlier the story was different. Operating cash flow was negative 73 crore in FY24 and negative 13 crore in FY25, although profit was positive both years. A profit that is not turning into cash is a warning, and one good year of conversion is evidence, not proof.

Finally, separate the spending from the parking. The cash flow summary shows investing outflows of about 253 crore in FY26. Most of that was fixed deposits, about 205 crore placed with banks. The plant spending on property, plant and equipment, work in progress and intangibles was about 49 crore. If you read the whole 253 crore as factory spending, you will overstate the company’s capital intensity by about five times. Keep those two lines apart as we move into the capital and returns chapters.

The raw-material question is a cash question as well as a margin question. With overseas suppliers and no long-term contract, the company pays for inputs at whatever the going rate is when it orders them. That gives it a reason to hold inventory, and inventory is cash that has not yet come back.

Think of FY26 in terms of a single rupee of revenue. Profit after tax was about ten paise of it. Operating cash was about nine paise, so nearly all of that profit arrived as cash in the year. The remaining gap is the part to watch, because it depends on inventory and receivables that have not yet been collected.

Ask one question every quarter: how much of the operating cash came from profit, and how much came from working capital releasing? Falling debtor days release cash only once. A company cannot keep releasing cash from the same receivables every year. Once the cycle has shortened, the next gain has to come from sales or margin, not from timing.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR’S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Imagine you are the person who has to pay the raw material bill next quarter, with no contract to protect you. Then ask whether the cash you have on hand covers that bill for as long as it takes to collect from customers. The answer tells you more about this business than the margin in any single quarter.
